lesson.title: The Chi-Square Statistic, Cell by Cell
lesson.summary: The chi-square statistic packages the gap between observed and expected counts, category by category, into one number that measures overall disagreement between data and a model.
lesson.body:
Once you have observed counts and a set of expected counts to compare them to, the chi-square statistic packages the comparison into a single number using this formula: X squared equals the sum, over every category or cell, of observed minus expected, squared, divided by expected.

Each piece of that formula is doing a specific job. The difference, observed minus expected, measures how far off a single category is. Squaring that difference does two things: it makes every term positive, so categories that ran too high and categories that ran too low both add to the total instead of canceling out, and it punishes big gaps more than small ones, since a gap of 10 contributes 100 to the numerator while a gap of 2 contributes only 4. Dividing by the expected count rescales that squared gap relative to how big the category was supposed to be in the first place: a gap of 5 is a huge deal in a category expected to have only 10 cases, but barely noticeable in a category expected to have 500. Finally, summing across every category folds all of that local information into one overall statistic that measures total disagreement between your data and whatever model produced the expected counts.

Here is a full worked example. A candy company claims its bags follow this color distribution: 30% brown, 20% yellow, 20% red, 10% orange, 10% green, 10% blue. A student opens a bag of 100 candies and counts 24 brown, 21 yellow, 19 red, 12 orange, 15 green, and 9 blue, which sum to 100, matching the sample size. Because the claim gives percentages and the sample size is 100, the expected count in each color is just the percentage applied to 100: 30 brown, 20 yellow, 20 red, 10 orange, 10 green, 10 blue, which also sum to 100.

Now compute observed minus expected, squared, divided by expected, one color at a time:
Brown: observed 24, expected 30, difference negative 6, squared 36, divided by 30 equals 1.20
Yellow: observed 21, expected 20, difference 1, squared 1, divided by 20 equals 0.05
Red: observed 19, expected 20, difference negative 1, squared 1, divided by 20 equals 0.05
Orange: observed 12, expected 10, difference 2, squared 4, divided by 10 equals 0.40
Green: observed 15, expected 10, difference 5, squared 25, divided by 10 equals 2.50
Blue: observed 9, expected 10, difference negative 1, squared 1, divided by 10 equals 0.10

Adding all six pieces: 1.20 plus 0.05 plus 0.05 plus 0.40 plus 2.50 plus 0.10 equals 4.30. So the chi-square statistic for this bag is X squared equals 4.30. Notice how the green cell contributed the most to the total, 2.50 out of 4.30, because it had the largest gap relative to its expected count. That kind of term-by-term breakdown is worth remembering, since it is the main tool for figuring out which categories drove a significant result later in this unit.

This exact recipe, subtract, square, divide by expected, sum, is used for every chi-square procedure you will meet: goodness-of-fit tests, tests for homogeneity, and tests for independence. What changes from one procedure to the next is only how the expected counts get calculated and how the degrees of freedom are determined, not the arithmetic itself. For this six-category goodness-of-fit example, the degrees of freedom would be the number of categories minus 1, or 5, which becomes important once you start turning this statistic into a P-value.
